Previously, EPIcode modeled only material with properties of neutral buoyancy and did not consider chemical materials with density greater than the ambient environment, dense gases. Materials exhibit dense gas properties when they are highly concentrated, and their resulting density is greater than that of the surrounding air. Though such circumstances are not long lived, they represent hazardous conditions requiring modeling and analysis at NNSA facilities. The high density of these materials results in a stronger influence from gravity in the vicinity of a dense gas source as depicted in the orange section of Fig. 1.1 and the region identified as S in Fig. 1.2. As a dense gas mixes with the surrounding air, its density transitions toward being more neutrally buoyant, neither heavier nor lighter than the ambient environment. This transition phase, which takes time and distance to evolve, is represented by the green plume in Fig. 1.1. The beginning of the transition phase of the actual dense gas plume in Fig. 1.2 is indicated as well. Figure 1.1. To broaden EPIcode’s capabilities, fulfill user needs, and satisfy a recommendation from DOE’s Safety Software Quality Assurance Central Registry under AU-32 within the Office of Environment, Health, Safety & Security (EHSS), it was important to develop a dense gas model. In the Spring of 2018, a proposal to incorporate a dense gas capability into EPIcode was accepted by the Nuclear Safety Research and Development (NSR&D) Program under EHSS. The effort to design, implement, and validate such a capability is summarized in this report. 5 LLNL-TR-818768 2 Design and Implementation of Dense Gas Capability The design and implementation effort addressed the following aspects of a dense gas release: • Criteria for determining when a material has denser than air properties at the source • Characterization of the dimensions and duration of the dense gas cloud • Transition from a dense gas phase toward neutrally buoyant conditions 2.1 Criteria for determining when a material has denser than air properties In order to establish a method for determining when a modeled gas or liquid release has denser than air properties, we conducted a literature review, looked at the approach in EPA’s dense gas model DEGADIS (Havens, et al., 1989), and conducted a peer review. The Release Richardson Number (Richardson Number or Ri ), a buoyancy indicator based on water tunnel experiments c by (Britter, 1980), was selected and incorporated into EPIcode. The Richardson Number (Eq. 1) is a common factor for characterizing atmospheric flows.
